abies.label: Fir

wikipedia.title: Fir
wikipedia.extract: Firs are evergreen coniferous trees belonging to the genus Abies in the family Pinaceae. There are approximately 48–65 extant species, found on mountains throughout much of North and Central America, Eurasia, and North Africa. The genus is most closely related to Keteleeria, a small genus confined to eastern Asia.

spotting: Needles attach singly and directly to the twig (no woody peg), leaving a smooth round scar when they fall.
Needles are flat, soft to the touch, and often have two pale stripes on the underside.
Cones stand upright on top branches like candles and disintegrate on the tree rather than falling whole.
Crown is a neat, narrow spire shape from base to tip.

acer.label: Maple

wikipedia.title: Maple
wikipedia.extract: Acer is a genus of trees and shrubs commonly known as maples. The genus is placed in the soapberry family Sapindaceae. There are approximately 132 species, most of which are native to East Asia, with a number also appearing in Europe, northern Africa, and North America.

spotting: Leaves and branching are opposite -- paired directly across from each other on the twig, not staggered.
Most leaves are palmately lobed, fanning out from one central point like fingers.
Paired winged seeds (samaras, 'helicopters') spin down in late summer.
Bark ranges from smooth and striped (young trees) to deeply furrowed and plated (old trunks), depending on species.

aesculus-hippocastanum.label: Chestnut

wikipedia.title: Aesculus hippocastanum
wikipedia.extract: Aesculus hippocastanum, the horse chestnut, is a species of flowering plant in the maple, soapberry and lychee family Sapindaceae. It is a large, deciduous, synoecious (hermaphroditic-flowered) tree. It is also called horse-chestnut, European horsechestnut, buckeye, and conker tree.

spotting: Leaves are palmately compound -- 5-7 leaflets fanning out from one point, like an open hand.
Large sticky, resinous buds in winter are a fast ID even with no leaves.
Upright cone-shaped clusters ('candles') of white flowers with pink or yellow throat markings in spring.
Fruit is a round, spiky green husk holding one or two glossy brown 'conkers'.

alnus.label: Alder

wikipedia.title: Alder
wikipedia.extract: Alders are trees of the genus Alnus in the birch family Betulaceae. The genus includes about 35 species of monoecious trees and shrubs, a few reaching a large size, distributed throughout the north temperate zone with a few species extending into Central America, as well as the northern and southern Andes.

spotting: Leaves are round-to-oval with a finely double-toothed edge and stay green late into fall, often falling while still green.
Small woody cone-like fruits (strobiles) persist on bare branches all winter -- a giveaway from across the street.
Bark is smooth and grey with pale horizontal lenticel scars, patched with lichen near rivers and ditches.

arbutus.label: Arbutus

wikipedia.title: Arbutus
wikipedia.extract: Arbutus is a genus of 12 accepted species of flowering plants in the family Ericaceae, native to temperate regions of the Mediterranean, western Europe, the Canary Islands and North America, and commonly called madrones, madronas, or strawberry trees. The name Arbutus was taken by taxonomists from Latin, where it referred to the species now designated Arbutus unedo.

spotting: Bark peels in curling papery sheets, showing smooth green-to-cinnamon new bark underneath -- unmistakable, no other tree on the coast does this.
Leaves are thick, glossy, leathery ovals that stay on the tree year-round (broadleaf evergreen).
Clusters of small urn-shaped white flowers in spring give way to bumpy orange-red berries in fall.
Often leans or twists dramatically, growing on rock outcrops with sparse, contorted limbs.

betula.label: Birch

wikipedia.title: Birch
wikipedia.extract: A birch is a thin-leaved deciduous hardwood tree of the genus Betula, in the family Betulaceae, which also includes alders, hazels, and hornbeams. It is closely related to the beech-oak family Fagaceae. The genus Betula contains 30 to 60 known taxa of which 11 are on the IUCN 2011 Red List of Threatened Species.

spotting: Bark is thin, smooth, and peels in horizontal papery strips -- white, silver, or coppery depending on species.
Trunk is often marked with dark, diamond-shaped lenticels.
Leaves are small, triangular-to-oval with a doubly-toothed edge and a pointed tip.
Slender drooping catkins hang from the branch tips in spring.

chamaecyparis.label: Cypress

wikipedia.title: Chamaecyparis
wikipedia.extract: Chamaecyparis, common names cypress or false cypress, is a genus of conifers in the cypress family Cupressaceae, native to eastern Asia and to the western and eastern margins of the United States. The name is derived from the Greek khamai (χαμαί), meaning "on the earth", and kuparissos (κυπάρισσος) for "cypress".

spotting: Foliage grows in flattened, fan-like sprays of tiny overlapping scales, drooping at the tips.
Undersides of the scale sprays often show a faint white X or butterfly marking of wax.
Small, round cones about the size of a pea, with shield-shaped scales.
Crown is often a narrow, drooping pyramid with a distinctly weeping leader.

cornus.label: Dogwood

wikipedia.title: Cornus
wikipedia.extract: Cornus is a genus of about 30–60 species of woody plants in the family Cornaceae, commonly known as dogwoods or cornels, which can generally be distinguished by their blossoms, berries, and distinctive bark. Most are deciduous trees or shrubs, but a few species are nearly herbaceous perennial subshrubs, and some species are evergreen. Several species have small heads of inconspicuous flowers surrounded by an...

spotting: Leaves are oval with strongly arching veins that curve to follow the leaf edge rather than crossing it.
Flowers on the flowering dogwoods are actually tiny true flowers surrounded by 4-6 large white or pink petal-like bracts.
Bark on mature trunks breaks into small, squarish blocks, sometimes compared to alligator skin.
Clusters of bright red berry-like drupes appear in late summer.

fraxinus.label: Ash

wikipedia.title: Fraxinus
wikipedia.extract: Fraxinus, commonly called ash, is a genus of plants in the olive and lilac family, Oleaceae, and comprises 45–65 species of usually medium-to-large trees, most of which are deciduous, although some subtropical species are evergreen. The genus is widespread throughout much of Europe, Asia, and North America.

spotting: Leaves are compound, with 5-9 leaflets arranged in opposite pairs along the stalk.
Twigs and buds are also strictly opposite -- look for two branches or buds directly across from each other.
Bark on mature trunks forms a tight diamond-shaped ridge pattern.
Seeds hang in dense clusters of single-wing 'keys' (samaras) that persist into winter.

juglans.label: Walnut

wikipedia.title: Walnut
wikipedia.extract: A walnut is the edible seed of any tree of the genus Juglans, particularly the Persian or English walnut, Juglans regia. They are accessory fruit because the outer covering of the fruit is technically an involucre and thus not morphologically part of the carpel; this means it cannot be a drupe but is instead a drupe-like nut.

spotting: Leaves are large compound leaves with 9-many leaflets, and crushed leaflets smell strongly aromatic (some describe it as spicy or medicinal).
Bark is dark grey-brown with deep, diamond-crossed furrows.
Fruit is a round green husk that blackens and stains hands and pavement, holding a hard corrugated nut inside.
Pith inside young twigs is chambered (segmented) rather than solid when cut lengthwise.

larix.label: Larch

wikipedia.title: Larch
wikipedia.extract: Larches are deciduous conifers in the genus Larix, of the family Pinaceae. Growing to as much as 60 m (195 ft) tall, they are native to the cooler regions of the Northern Hemisphere. They grow in lowland forests in the far north, and high in mountains further south.

spotting: Needles grow in dense whorled tufts on short spur shoots, unlike other conifers on the street.
It's a deciduous conifer -- needles turn gold and drop completely every fall, leaving bare branches all winter.
Small, upright barrel-shaped cones persist on the twigs long after the needles are gone.

magnolia.label: Magnolia

wikipedia.title: Magnolia
wikipedia.extract: Magnolia is a large genus of about 210 to 340 flowering plant species in the subfamily Magnolioideae of the family Magnoliaceae. The natural range of Magnolia species is disjunct, with a main center in east, south and southeast Asia and a secondary center in South America, Central America, the West Indies, and some species in eastern North America.

spotting: Leaves are large, simple, untoothed ovals with a leathery feel.
Flowers are large (often hand-sized), cup- or star-shaped, in white, pink or purple, opening before or with the leaves.
Flower buds are covered in a distinctive soft, fuzzy grey scale through winter.
Cone-like seed pods split open to reveal bright red-orange seeds hanging on thin threads.

picea.label: Spruce

wikipedia.title: Spruce
wikipedia.extract: A spruce is a tree of the genus Picea, a genus of some 37 species of coniferous evergreen trees in the family Pinaceae, found in the northern temperate and boreal (taiga) regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Picea is treated either in the subfamily Pinoideae, or the sole genus in its own subfamily Piceoideae.

spotting: Needles attach singly to small woody pegs (sterigmata) that remain on the twig after needles drop -- twigs feel rough and bumpy when needles are stripped off.
Needles are stiff, four-sided, and sharp to the touch when rolled between fingers.
Cones hang down and drop whole to the ground, unlike upright fir cones.
Crown is a strict, symmetrical spire from young age.

pinus.label: Pine

wikipedia.title: Pine
wikipedia.extract: A pine is any conifer in the genus Pinus of the family Pinaceae. Pinus is the sole genus in the subfamily Pinoideae. The species are evergreen trees or shrubs with their leaves in bunches, usually of 2 to 5 needles.

spotting: Needles are long, grow in bundles (fascicles) of 2, 3 or 5 depending on species, bound at the base by a papery sheath.
Cones are woody with thick, often prickly scales, and take two seasons to mature.
Bark on older trunks breaks into irregular plates or scaly ridges, often orange-brown in the furrows.

populus.label: Poplar

wikipedia.title: Populus
wikipedia.extract: Populus is a genus of 25–30 species of deciduous flowering plants in the family Salicaceae, native to most of the Northern Hemisphere. English names variously applied to different species include poplar, aspen, and cottonwood.

spotting: Leaves flutter and shimmer in the slightest breeze -- the flattened leaf stalk (petiole) lets them twist freely.
Bark on young trees is smooth and pale, often greenish-white, with diamond-shaped scars; older bark becomes deeply furrowed near the base.
Fast, tall, narrow growth habit with a straight trunk and relatively sparse crown.
Catkins (not showy flowers) appear before the leaves in early spring; some species release cottony seed fluff in early summer.

prunus.label: Cherry

wikipedia.title: Cherry
wikipedia.extract: A cherry is the fruit of many plants of the genus Prunus, and is a fleshy drupe.

spotting: Bark is smooth and reddish-brown to grey, marked with distinct horizontal lines (lenticels).
Flowers arrive in dense clusters before or with the leaves -- white to deep pink, often frilly and double on street trees.
Leaves have a fine, single-toothed (serrated) edge and a pointed tip.
Small round stone fruit; on ornamental cultivars flowers are showy but fruit is often sparse or absent.

prunus-laurocerasus.label: Laurel

wikipedia.title: Prunus laurocerasus
wikipedia.extract: Prunus laurocerasus, also known as cherry laurel, common laurel and sometimes English laurel in North America, is an evergreen species of cherry (Prunus), native to regions bordering the Black Sea in southwestern Asia and southeastern Europe, from Albania and Bulgaria east through Turkey to the Caucasus Mountains and northern Iran.

spotting: Leaves are broad, glossy, leathery ovals that stay on the plant year-round -- a broadleaf evergreen among mostly deciduous street trees.
Leaf edges are smooth or very finely toothed, not deeply serrated.
Small white flowers stand up in narrow upright spikes, followed by small cherry-like black fruit.
Often kept clipped into a dense hedge or screen rather than grown as a single-trunked tree.

quercus.label: Oak

wikipedia.title: Oak
wikipedia.extract: An oak is a hardwood tree or shrub in the genus Quercus of the beech family. They have spirally arranged leaves, often with lobed edges, and a nut called an acorn, borne within a cup. The genus is widely distributed in the Northern Hemisphere, with some 500 species, both deciduous and evergreen.

spotting: Leaves are lobed (rounded or bristle-tipped, depending on species) with an asymmetric, wavy outline.
Acorns in a scaly cup are unmistakable when present, late summer into fall.
Bark is thick, grey, and deeply furrowed into rough vertical ridges even on medium-sized trunks.
Heavy, wide-spreading limbs give the crown a broad, rounded silhouette.

salix.label: Willow

wikipedia.title: Willow
wikipedia.extract: Willows, also called sallows and osiers, of the genus Salix, comprise around 350 species of typically deciduous trees and shrubs. They are primarily found on moist soils in cold and temperate regions.

spotting: Leaves are long, narrow, and several times longer than they are wide, often with a silvery underside.
Twigs are slender and whippy, and on many species droop or sweep downward.
Bark is grey and becomes deeply furrowed with age; trees are usually found near water or damp ground.
Furry grey catkins ('pussy willows') appear on bare branches before the leaves in very early spring.

taxus.label: Yew

wikipedia.title: Taxus
wikipedia.extract: Taxus is a genus of coniferous trees or shrubs known as yews in the family Taxaceae. Yews occur around the globe in temperate zones of the northern hemisphere, northernmost in Norway and southernmost in the South Celebes. Some populations exist in tropical highlands.

spotting: Needles are flat, dark green, soft (not prickly), and arranged in two flat ranks along the twig.
Bark is thin and reddish-brown, peeling in small flakes or scales.
No true cones -- instead, single seeds sit in a bright red, soft, cup-shaped berry-like structure (aril) in fall.
Foliage and seeds are highly toxic if eaten -- a fact worth knowing, not just spotting.

thuja-plicata.label: Cedar

wikipedia.title: Thuja plicata
wikipedia.extract: Thuja plicata is a large evergreen coniferous tree in the family Cupressaceae, native to the Pacific Northwest of North America. Its common name is western redcedar. It is also less commonly called western red cedar, pacific red cedar, giant arborvitae, western arborvitae, just cedar, giant cedar, or shinglewood.

spotting: Foliage grows in flat, drooping sprays of tiny scale-like leaves, not individual needles.
Crushed foliage smells strongly of pineapple or fresh-cut cedar.
Bark is stringy and fibrous, tearing into long vertical strips rather than flaking or plating.
Small cones are woody, egg-shaped and no bigger than a thumbnail, in loose clusters near branch tips.

tsuga.label: Hemlock

wikipedia.title: Tsuga
wikipedia.extract: Tsuga is a genus of conifers in the subfamily Abietoideae of Pinaceae, the pine family. The English-language common name "hemlock" arose from a perceived similarity in the smell of its crushed foliage to that of the unrelated plant hemlock. Unlike the latter, Tsuga species are not poisonous.

spotting: Needles are short, flat, and irregular in length along the twig, giving sprays a soft, feathery look.
The leading shoot at the very top of the tree droops over instead of standing upright -- the single most reliable field mark.
Small cones hang down and are barely bigger than a fingertip.
Needles have two white stripes underneath and a tiny stalk where they meet the twig.

ulmus.label: Elm

wikipedia.title: Elm
wikipedia.extract: Elms are deciduous and semi-deciduous trees comprising the genus Ulmus in the family Ulmaceae. They are distributed over most of the Northern Hemisphere, inhabiting the temperate and tropical-montane regions of North America and Eurasia, ranging southward in Western Asia to Iran, in Africa to Libya, and in Southeast Asia into Indonesia.

spotting: Leaf bases are lopsided -- one side meets the stem lower than the other.
Bark is grey-brown with deep interlacing ridges like braided rope.
Branches arch up and out into a broad vase silhouette.
Flat, round, papery winged seeds (samaras) appear in dense clusters before the leaves in spring.
